title: What is consistent hashing, how does it minimize data movement when adding/removing nodes (only K/N keys move instead of all), and what is a virtual node (multiple hash positions per physical node for better balance)?

s1_definition.profdef: Consistent hashing maps both keys and nodes onto a fixed circular hash space (the ring); each key belongs to the first node found clockwise. When a node is added or removed, only the keys between it and its neighbor move — about K over N keys — instead of nearly all keys as with modulo hashing. A virtual node is one of several ring positions assigned to the same physical node, which smooths out uneven distribution and makes rebalancing finer-grained.
s1_definition.analogy: Imagine National Bank of India placing all accounts around a clock face, and each shard also sits at a spot on the clock; an account is handled by the next shard clockwise. If the bank opens a new shard, only the accounts in that one arc move to it — everyone else stays put. Virtual nodes are like giving each shard many spots around the clock so no single shard accidentally ends up with a giant arc of accounts.
s1_definition.oneliner: Consistent hashing moves only K/N keys when nodes change, and virtual nodes give each physical node many ring spots for even balance.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Consistent hashing maps both keys and nodes onto a fixed circular hash space (the ring); each key belongs to the first node found clockwise. When a node is added or removed, only the keys between it and its neighbor move — about K over N keys — instead of nearly all keys as with modulo hashing. A virtual node is one of several ring positions assigned to the same physical node, which smooths out uneven distribution and makes rebalancing finer-grained.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Imagine National Bank of India placing all accounts around a clock face, and each shard also sits at a spot on the clock; an account is handled by the next shard clockwise. If the bank opens a new shard, only the accounts in that one arc move to it — everyone else stays put. Virtual nodes are like giving each shard many spots around the clock so no single shard accidentally ends up with a giant arc of accounts.

**One line to remember:** Consistent hashing moves only K/N keys when nodes change, and virtual nodes give each physical node many ring spots for even balance.

sections.s2_technical:
With plain modulo hashing `shard = hash(key) % N`, changing N changes almost every assignment, so adding one node reshuffles nearly all data — catastrophic for a live system. Consistent hashing fixes this by hashing nodes and keys onto the same ring; a key is owned by the first node clockwise. Adding a node inserts one point on the ring and steals only the arc between it and the previous node; removing a node hands its arc to the next node. So only the fraction K over N of keys move.

The problem with few points per node is uneven arcs — one node can own a much larger slice by chance, creating a hotspot. Virtual nodes solve this: each physical node is hashed to many positions (for example 150), so its ownership is spread into many small arcs that average out to an even share, and heterogeneous nodes can be weighted by giving bigger ones more virtual nodes.

Senior nuance: consistent hashing underpins distributed caches and databases (Dynamo-style systems, Cassandra, many Redis clusters). It also enables replication by walking clockwise to the next N distinct physical nodes. Pick enough virtual nodes to keep load variance low, and use a good hash to avoid clustering.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — National Bank of India must add a shard without reshuffling all accounts and without creating a hot shard. This is exactly consistent hashing with virtual nodes: adding a node moves only one arc, and virtual nodes keep the arcs even.

The demo has a `ConsistentHashRing` with `addNode()`, `removeNode()`, and `route()`, using virtual nodes, and shows that adding a shard relocates only Rajesh's or Priya's key if it falls in the new arc, counting how many keys move.

##### 4b. SQL Database Script

```sql
-- V1__ring_note.sql (routing lives in app/proxy; shards share schema)
-- Each physical shard owns MANY ring positions (virtual nodes) for even balance.
-- Adding shard_3 moves only the keys in shard_3's new arcs (~K/N), not all keys.
CREATE TABLE accounts (
    id      VARCHAR(20) PRIMARY KEY,
    balance DECIMAL(15,2) NOT NULL
);
```

##### 4c. Configuration File

```yaml
# application.yml
consistent-hash:
  physical-nodes: [shard_0, shard_1, shard_2]
  virtual-nodes-per-node: 150     # higher = smoother balance
  replication-walk: 3             # next 3 distinct nodes clockwise
```

sections.s5_journey:
Input: three shards each with 150 virtual nodes, and five account keys routed before and after adding a fourth shard.

Step 1: Each shard is hashed to 150 ring positions, so the five keys spread fairly evenly across shard_0, shard_1, and shard_2.

Step 2: Adding shard_3 inserts 150 new positions; only keys that now find shard_3 as the first node clockwise move, which is a small fraction — roughly one of the five.

Step 3: The demo counts exactly how many keys moved, demonstrating the K-over-N property rather than a full reshuffle.

sections.s5b_flow:
```text
  Hash ring (0 .. 2^32)
    ● shard_0 (×150 vnodes)   ● shard_1 (×150)   ● shard_2 (×150)
    key → first node clockwise
    │
    ▼ add shard_3 (×150 vnodes)
    only keys in shard_3's new arcs move  (≈ K/N)
    others stay on their original node
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
Consistent hashing maps both the keys and the nodes onto a single circular hash space, and each key is owned by the first node found clockwise from the key's position. The payoff is that when I add or remove a node, only the keys in that node's arc move — about K over N of all keys — instead of the near-total reshuffle that plain modulo hashing causes when the node count changes, which makes online scaling practical. A virtual node is one of many ring positions assigned to the same physical node; by giving each physical node many positions, its ownership is split into many small arcs that average out to an even share, which prevents one node from accidentally owning a huge slice and lets me weight bigger nodes with more virtual positions.

In our National Bank of India sharded accounts I route by account id on a consistent-hash ring with around 150 virtual nodes per shard, so load stays even and adding a shard relocates only the small fraction of accounts that fall into the new shard's arcs rather than every account. The same ring also gives me replication for free by walking clockwise to the next few distinct physical nodes. This is the technique behind Dynamo-style stores, Cassandra, and many distributed caches. The line I remember is: consistent hashing moves only K over N keys when nodes change, and virtual nodes give each physical node many ring spots so the load stays balanced.
